Nicholas II. The last tsar of Russia, he presided over a doomed empire during the final age of autocracy. Weak-willed, indecisive, and devoted to the principle of absolute power, he refused meaningful reform despite military defeat, economic crisis, and revolutionary ferment. He embodies the failure of autocracy in the modern age.

He ascended in 1894 after his father Alexander III's death. Initially well-intentioned but fatally indecisive, he inherited his father's reactionary policies and commitment to absolute autocracy despite the empire's desperate need for reform. He married Alexandra of Hesse-Darmstadt, a German princess devoted to Orthodoxy and autocracy, and she reinforced his conservative instincts at every turn. He appointed ineffectual and reactionary advisors, blocking progressive voices in the government.

The turning point came with military disaster. He waged the Russo-Japanese War between 1904 and 1905, and Russia was defeated by a non-European power for the first time, exposing imperial weakness to the world. Military defeat triggered the Revolution of 1905. Workers' strikes, peasant unrest, and military mutiny shook the empire. He was forced to issue the October Manifesto in 1905, reluctantly promising civil liberties and a representative assembly called the Duma. But he spent the following years slowly undermining nearly every concession he had made.

He allowed Prime Minister Pyotr Stolypin to implement controversial reforms between 1906 and 1911, yet resisted constitutional limitations on his power at every step. The Duma functioned as a powerless advisory body. Nicholas repeatedly dissolved it when it opposed his will. Political factions—liberals, socialists, conservatives—battled while the executive remained immobile and autocratic.

Stolypin's assassination in 1911 removed the one capable reformer. Nicholas sank into passivity and religious mysticism. Court intrigues intensified around Grigory Rasputin, a self-proclaimed holy man who gained influence over the empress and the sickly heir.

Then came World War I. Nicholas entered the war in 1914, confident in Russian strength. Instead, the war exposed the empire's military, economic, and logistical weakness. He took personal command of the army in 1915, leaving government to the empress and Rasputin. Administrative collapse followed. Military losses mounted. By 1916 and 1917, millions of soldiers were dead or wounded. Food shortages and inflation devastated the home front.

Nicholas resigned under pressure in March 1917. The Bolsheviks seized power in October. He and his entire family—his wife and five children—were executed by the Bolsheviks on July 17, 1918, in Yekaterinburg, ending three centuries of Romanov rule.

Nicholas II is a tragic figure. Not evil, but fatally unsuited to power during revolutionary change. He inherited a system of absolute autocracy when the world moved toward democracy. His refusal to share power, his indecision, his reliance on reactionary advisors made him the last tsar not because he was uniquely terrible, but because he represented a system that could no longer sustain itself.
